question: How much FMLA leave am I actually entitled to?
rule:
Twelve workweeks in a twelve-month period, and this is now the statute's own words rather than a court's description of them. 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a)(1): “Subject to section 2613 of this title and subsection (d)(3), an eligible employee shall be entitled to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for one or more of the following:” The list that follows covers birth, placement for adoption or foster care, care for a spouse, son, daughter or parent with a serious health condition, and the employee's own serious health condition. Leave under the Act is unpaid, and the entitlement is a ceiling as well as a floor: the Supreme Court in Ragsdale v. Wolverine World Wide called it the Act's most fundamental substantive guarantee and held that an employer which had already given thirty weeks owed no more. Who is an ‘eligible employee’ is defined in § 2611(2)(A): “The term “eligible employee” means an employee who has been employed—
(i) for at least 12 months by the employer with respect to whom leave is requested under section 2612 of this title; and
(ii) for at least 1,250 hours of service with such employer during the previous 12-month period.”
trap: People read the twelve weeks as a minimum the employer must add to whatever leave it already gave. Ragsdale is the case that says otherwise: the employee there received 30 weeks of leave, more than twice the Act requires, and still argued she was owed 12 more because of a notice failure. She lost. If your employer's own policy is more generous than the Act, the extra weeks can be counted against the twelve, and the fight is about whether the leave was properly designated, not about whether you got enough of it.

question: My employer never told me my time off counted as FMLA leave. Do I get another twelve weeks?
rule: Not by itself. A Department of Labor regulation once said exactly that — that leave not designated as FMLA leave does not count against the entitlement — and the Supreme Court struck it down. We hold that the regulation is contrary to the Act and beyond the Secretary of Labor's authority. Ragsdale was entitled to no more leave, and Wolverine was entitled to summary judgment. The Court's reason was about who has to prove what: The challenged regulation is invalid because it alters the FMLA's cause of action in a fundamental way: It relieves employees of the burden of proving any real impairment of their rights and resulting prejudice.
trap: The trap is treating the employer's paperwork failure as the violation. Under Ragsdale it is not: you still have to show the failure actually cost you something — that you would have arranged your leave differently, or taken it at another time, or otherwise been left worse off. An employer that handled the notice badly but gave you every week you were entitled to has, on these facts, given you your remedy already. Bring the prejudice, not just the missing form.

question: I work for the state. Can I actually sue my employer for money under the FMLA?
rule:
It depends which kind of leave. For family-care leave — caring for a spouse, child or parent — the Supreme Court held in Nevada Department of Human Resources v. Hibbs that Congress validly removed the States' immunity: We hold that employees of the State of Nevada may recover money damages in the event of the State's failure to comply with the family-care provision of the Act. For self-care leave — your own serious health condition — the Court held the opposite in Coleman v. Court of Appeals of Maryland: But the provision, standing
    alone, is not a valid abrogation of the States’ immunity from suit.
trap: This split catches people who read one case and stop. Two employees at the same state agency, both denied FMLA leave, can have completely different remedies: the one who took leave to care for a parent may sue the State for damages, and the one who took leave for their own illness may not. Note also what this is NOT about. It is about suing a STATE employer for money. It says nothing about private employers, where sovereign immunity is not in the picture at all, and a reader who concludes that self-care leave is unprotected generally has misread it.

question: How long do I have to file a discrimination charge, and when does the clock start?
rule: Title VII requires a charge with the EEOC before a lawsuit, and the period is short. 42 U.S.C. § 2000e–5(e)(1): “A charge under this section shall be filed within one hundred and eighty days after the alleged unlawful employment practice occurred” The same subsection sets a longer period where a state or local fair-employment agency exists, which Mohasco Corp. v. Silver quotes as “such charge shall be filed by or on behalf of the person aggrieved within three hundred days after the alleged unlawful employment practice occurred,” with a further limb tying it to the end of the state proceeding.
trap: The clock starts when you are TOLD, not when it hurts. Ricks is the case: a professor was notified he would get a terminal one-year contract, worked that year, and filed after his employment actually ended. Too late — the limitations period ran from the notice of the decision, not from the day the consequences arrived. If you have been told your job ends on a future date, assume the clock is already running today.

question: Is there a federal law about non-competes?
rule: We hold no verified federal authority on non-compete agreements. This is a finding about our corpus, not about the world: the federal tier we publish is Supreme Court opinions, and none of the opinions we hold states a general federal rule on the enforceability of a non-compete. Rules affecting non-competes have come from agencies rather than from the Court, and we do not hold the Code of Federal Regulations.
trap: Do not read the silence as “non-competes are fine federally”. Read it as: ask about your STATE, which is where the answer has historically lived, and this pack holds a verified Washington rule.
notes: Recorded deliberately. The schema this pack follows says a missing row and a padded row are both worse than an honest empty one, because a missing row reads as “nothing to say here” and a padded row reads as law.

question: My employer made taking FMLA leave difficult, or punished me for it. What exactly is unlawful?
rule: Two separate things, and they are not the same claim. Interference, 29 U.S.C. § 2615(a)(1): “It shall be unlawful for any employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this subchapter.” And discrimination for opposing, § 2615(a)(2): “It shall be unlawful for any employer to discharge or in any other manner discriminate against any individual for opposing any practice made unlawful by this subchapter.” Subsection (b) adds a third, protecting anyone who has filed a charge, instituted a proceeding, given information in an inquiry, or testified.
trap: The two are pleaded differently and people collapse them. Interference asks whether you were denied something the Act gave you, and the employer's motive is not part of that sentence. Discrimination under (a)(2) asks whether you were punished for OPPOSING a practice made unlawful, which is about what the employer was reacting to. So an employee who was simply refused leave has an interference claim without ever proving animus, and an employee who complained and was then fired is in (a)(2) or (b) territory. Note also who (b) binds: it says ‘any person’, not ‘any employer’, which is a wider word than the rest of the section uses.

question: If my employer broke the FMLA, what can I actually recover?
rule: Lost pay, interest, the same amount again, and your job back. 29 U.S.C. § 2617(a)(1)(A) makes an employer who violates § 2615 liable for “any wages, salary, employment benefits, or other compensation denied or lost to such employee by reason of the violation;” plus interest at the prevailing rate, plus “an additional amount as liquidated damages equal to the sum of the amount described in clause (i) and the interest described in clause (ii), except that if an employer who has violated section 2615 of this title proves to the satisfaction of the court that the act or omission which violated section 2615 of this title was in good faith and that the employer had reasonable grounds for believing that the act or omission was not a violation of section 2615 of this title, such court may, in the discretion of the court, reduce the amount of the liability to the amount and interest determined under clauses (i) and (ii), respectively;” And § 2617(a)(1)(B) adds liability “for such equitable relief as may be appropriate, including employment, reinstatement, and promotion.” Where no pay was lost, the same paragraph measures actual monetary losses such as the cost of providing care, capped at twelve weeks of wages, or twenty-six for servicemember-care leave.
trap: Read the liquidated-damages sentence in the right direction. Doubling is the DEFAULT, not a penalty a court adds for bad behaviour: the employer gets back to single damages only by proving both good faith and reasonable grounds for believing it was not violating the Act, and even then the reduction is discretionary rather than automatic. That is the opposite of how most damages provisions read, and it is why the size of an FMLA claim is often twice what an employee first calculates.

question: How long do I have to sue under the FMLA, and do I have to go to an agency first?
rule: Two years, three if the violation was wilful, and you do not need an agency charge first. 29 U.S.C. § 2617(c)(1): “an action may be brought under this section not later than 2 years after the date of the last event constituting the alleged violation for which the action is brought.” And § 2617(c)(2): “In the case of such action brought for a willful violation of section 2615 of this title, such action may be brought within 3 years of the date of the last event constituting the alleged violation for which such action is brought.” The right of action in § 2617(a)(2) lets an employee bring the action directly in any Federal or State court of competent jurisdiction.
trap: This is a DIFFERENT clock from the discrimination charge deadline in this pack, and confusing them cuts both ways. Someone who assumes the short charge period applies to an FMLA claim may give up a claim that was still alive for years. Someone who assumes the two-year FMLA period covers a discrimination claim will miss the charge deadline entirely. Note also where this clock starts: the last event constituting the alleged violation, which is its own question and not the same as the day you were told.
